This projection is part of a broader economic forecast that extends through 2028 and considers the impact of new policies. <4> The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) announced that the U-6 unemployment rate, a broader measure of labor underutilization, increased to 8.1% in August 2025 from 7.9% in July. This rate, which is released alongside the standard unemployment rate, includes not only the unemployed but also discouraged workers and individuals working part-time for economic reasons. The standard unemployment rate (U-3) saw a slight increase to 4.3% in August. The number of individuals employed part-time for economic reasons, who would prefer full-time work, was a significant component of the U-6 figure, totaling 4.7 million people in August. <5> The August 2025 jobs report, released on September 5, 2025, provided unemployment rates for various industries. Employment in the broader categories of financial activities and manufacturing showed little change in August. <6> On September 5, 2025, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics released its Employment Situation report for August 2025. The report indicated that the number of long-term unemployed individuals (those jobless for 27 weeks or more) was 1.9 million. The overall unemployment rate in August 2025 was 4.3%, with 7.4 million people unemployed in total. <7> In its analysis of the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' (BLS) August 2025 jobs report, the AFL-CIO highlighted that the Black unemployment rate rose to 7.5%. The overall unemployment rate in the U.S. held at 4.3%, with the economy adding 22,000 nonfarm payroll jobs. <10> The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported that the unemployment rate for August 2025 was 4.3%, a slight increase from 4.2% in the previous month. A subsequent final estimate released in early November revised these figures slightly, projecting an October unemployment rate of approximately 4.36%, up from about 4.35% in September. These real-time forecasts, which combine private sector data with estimates of the missing government statistics, became a critical source of information for policymakers and investors during the data blackout. <6> The Department of Labor reported that for the week ending September 20, 2025, initial jobless claims in the United States were 218,000. This represented a decrease of 14,000 from the previous week's figure of 232,000 and was well below the market consensus forecast of 235,000. The lower-than-expected number suggested some short-term stability and pushed back against recent concerns of an aggressive deterioration in the labor market. <7> On September 19, 2025, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics released state-level employment and unemployment data for August 2025, highlighting significant regional disparities. The report indicated that South Dakota had the lowest jobless rate at 1.9 percent. In contrast, the District of Columbia had the highest unemployment rate at 6.0 percent, followed by California at 5.5 percent. The national unemployment rate for August was 4.3 percent, and a total of 22 states had unemployment rates below this national figure. <8> During its meeting on September 16-17, 2025, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) released its Summary of Economic Projections. In these projections, the median forecast among FOMC participants for the unemployment rate for the fourth quarter of 2025 was 4.5%. This projection was part of a broader set of forecasts for key economic indicators, including GDP growth and inflation, for the years 2025 through 2028 and into the longer run. The projections are based on each participant's assessment of appropriate monetary policy at the time of the meeting. The announcement of these projections was made on September 17, 2025. <9> The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) projects the unemployment rate will reach 4.5% in the fourth quarter of 2025. This forecast anticipates a softening of the labor market due to weaker aggregate demand, influenced by factors such as tariffs. The CBO's September 2025 economic outlook also noted that slower growth in 2025 is a primary driver of this trend. This projection is part of a broader economic forecast that extends through 2028 and considers the impact of new policies. <10> The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) announced that the U-6 unemployment rate, a broader measure of labor underutilization, increased to 8.1% in August 2025 from 7.9% in July. This rate, which is released alongside the standard unemployment rate, includes not only the unemployed but also discouraged workers and individuals working part-time for economic reasons. The standard unemployment rate (U-3) saw a slight increase to 4.3% in August. The number of individuals employed part-time for economic reasons, who would prefer full-time work, was a significant component of the U-6 figure, totaling 4.7 million people in August.
